notes: COPEI is the ruling party (Caldera, minority government since March 1969); there was no formal coalition on 1 Jan 1970, so slot 2 holds URD as the most coalition-prone centrist party. AD moved from MD slot 18 to slot 3 (starting popularity); MEP takes slot 18. Pérez Jiménez's CCN in slot 20. MAS appears as second period of slot 5 (PCV split, founded 19 Jan 1971).

0.name: Dirección de los Servicios de Inteligencia y Prevención
0.english: Directorate of Intelligence and Prevention Services
0.native_full: Dirección de los Servicios de Inteligencia y Prevención
0.text:
The DISIP is the political police created by President Caldera in March 1969 to replace the discredited DIGEPOL. It inherits a decade of counterinsurgency against the guerrillas of the 1960s, its files, its interrogation cells and close working ties with American advisers.

Within the state it is the stronghold of those who believe democracy survives only by a firm hand: surveillance of the left, preventive arrests and quiet cooperation with Washington against Cuban influence. Its leverage lies in secrets, in its reach into the universities and unions, and in the fear that the pacification of the guerrillas may fail and its methods will be needed again.

1.name: Comité de Organización Política Electoral Independiente
1.native_full: Comité de Organización Política Electoral Independiente
1.text:
COPEI, founded in 1946 by Rafael Caldera, is Venezuela's Christian Democratic party. Caldera's narrow victory in December 1968 brought the first peaceful handover of power from one party to another in Venezuelan history, and since March 1969 COPEI governs as a minority, relying on shifting agreements in Congress, above all with Acción Democrática.

The party preaches social Christian humanism, cooperation between capital and labour and a pluralist democracy. Caldera's government pursues the pacification of the guerrillas, legalising the Communist Party, and an independent foreign policy of 'international social justice' that opens relations with Moscow while staying anchored to the West. Its base lies in the Andean states, the Catholic middle classes and a growing youth movement.

2.name: Unión Republicana Democrática
2.text:
The URD, founded in 1945 and led ever since by the orator Jóvito Villalba, is one of the three signatories of the 1958 Pact of Punto Fijo. It governed alongside AD in the early 1960s and backed Miguel Ángel Burelli Rivas in 1968, finishing well behind the two big parties; in 1970 it sits in opposition to Caldera.

URD presents itself as a centrist, progressive and nationalist force, friendly to private enterprise yet critical of foreign oil companies and of AD's party machine. Its strength rests on Villalba's personal following in the east, on urban professionals and on its role as a swing partner in Congress for any government lacking a majority.

3.name: Acción Democrática
3.text:
Acción Democrática, the party of Rómulo Betancourt and Raúl Leoni, built Venezuelan democracy after 1958 and governed for a decade. Weakened by the 1967 split that produced the MEP, it lost the 1968 presidential race by a hair and is now the largest opposition party, led by Gonzalo Barrios with Carlos Andrés Pérez rising in its ranks.

AD stands for agrarian reform, state control over oil revenue, strong unions and a firmly anti-communist, pro-American democracy. Its machinery reaches every village through the Confederation of Workers and the peasant federation. Holding the largest bloc in Congress, it can make or break Caldera's legislation and expects to return to power in 1973.

4.name: Partido Comunista de Venezuela
4.text:
The PCV, founded in 1931, was outlawed in 1962 after joining the armed struggle, and abandoned the guerrilla road in 1967. Legalised again under Caldera's pacification policy in 1969, it is led by veterans such as Gustavo Machado and Jesús Faría, but is torn by a bitter internal debate over the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The party follows Moscow's line: peaceful transition, a broad anti-imperialist front, nationalisation of oil and iron, and friendship with the Soviet Union and Cuba. Its base lies in the oil workers, parts of the student movement and Caracas intellectuals, but the dissidence of Teodoro Petkoff and Pompeyo Márquez threatens to take its youth away.

5.name: Los Renovadores
5.text:
The Renovators are the rebellious wing of the Communist Party around Teodoro Petkoff and Pompeyo Márquez, both veterans of the guerrilla years. Petkoff's book condemning the invasion of Czechoslovakia has made them heretics in the eyes of the old guard and of Moscow.

They call for a Venezuelan socialism free of Soviet tutelage, democratic, open to the new student radicalism of 1968 and rooted in national conditions rather than imported dogma. Their following among young cadres, university militants and former guerrillas is large, and a break with the PCV leadership looks only a matter of time.

5.name: Movimiento al Socialismo
5.text:
The Movement for Socialism is founded in January 1971 by the dissidents who walked out of the Communist Party, led by Teodoro Petkoff and Pompeyo Márquez. It takes most of the PCV's youth with it and quickly becomes the main force of the Venezuelan left.

MAS rejects both the Soviet model and guerrilla adventurism, and proposes a 'new socialism' built through elections, unions, universities and local organisation. It denounces the imperialism of both superpowers and seeks to break the two-party dominance of AD and COPEI, drawing on students, intellectuals and a new generation of urban professionals.

6.name: Los Nacionalistas del Petróleo
6.text:
The Oil Nationalists are a loose network of economists, officers, lawyers and senior officials who believe that the foreign concessions of Creole, Shell and Gulf are an affront to sovereignty. They draw on the ideas of Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo, co-founder of OPEC, and on a long tradition of hostility to the companies.

They demand higher taxes, the reversion of concessions and ultimately full nationalisation, and they look admiringly to Libya, Algeria and Peru. Distrustful of Washington and of the business federations, they have influence in the Ministry of Mines, the armed forces and Congress, where any vote on oil can rally deputies from all parties.

7.name: Oficiales del Carupanazo
7.text:
The Officers of the Carupanazo are the heirs of the leftist naval and army revolts of Carúpano and Puerto Cabello in 1962. Many of the rebels were killed, jailed or passed to the guerrillas, but sympathisers survive in the barracks and the military academies.

Inspired by the revolutionary military government in Peru since 1968, they dream of officers who would sweep away the parties, nationalise oil and align Venezuela with the anti-imperialist camp. Their numbers are small and the high command watches them closely, but disillusion with civilian politics gives their ideas a hearing among young lieutenants.

8.name: Los Amigos de Musa Sadr
8.text:
The Friends of Musa Sadr are Lebanese Shia merchants and shopkeepers of Margarita Island, Caracas and Valencia who follow the career of Imam Musa al-Sadr, head of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Lebanon since 1969. They gather in homes and family associations rather than mosques.

They favour a modern, socially engaged Shia identity that defends the deprived of southern Lebanon without breaking with the state. In Venezuela they keep a low profile, send remittances home and stay loyal to the democratic order that lets their businesses prosper, their only leverage being money and family networks.

9.name: Círculo de Nayaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a handful of young Lebanese Shia in Venezuela who correspond with seminary students in Najaf, where the exiled Iranian cleric Ruhollah Khomeini is lecturing on government by the jurist. They meet for religious study and circulate pamphlets brought from Iraq and Lebanon.

They regard both the American and the Soviet systems as godless and see the Shah and Israel as enemies of the faith. With no mosque, no funds and no standing in the wider community, they are an insignificant fringe, but they cultivate a militant piety that rejects quietism.

10.name: La Mezquita de los Comerciantes
10.text:
The Merchants' Mosque is the informal congregation of Sunni Syrian, Lebanese and Palestinian traders in Caracas, Valencia and Punto Fijo. Prayers are held in rented rooms and private homes, and its elders hope for Saudi support to build a proper mosque.

It teaches an orthodox, politically quiet Islam that respects authority, avoids controversy and keeps the community respectable in a Catholic country. Its members are pragmatic businessmen who value good relations with Venezuelan governments and with the conservative monarchies of the Gulf, from which they import religious books and preachers.

11.name: Los Estudiantes del Tahrir
11.text:
The Tahrir Students are a small study cell of Arab students at the Central University of Venezuela inspired by the Hizb ut-Tahrir of Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, founded in Jerusalem in 1953. They meet secretly and translate pamphlets from Beirut and Amman.

They reject nationalism, Ba'athism and Western democracy alike, and call for a restored caliphate uniting all Muslims under Islamic law. Isolated even among Venezuela's Muslims, they have no influence beyond a few dozen sympathisers, though the defeat of 1967 has made their message more appealing to angry young Arabs.

12.name: Los Hermanos de Alepo
12.text:
The Brothers of Aleppo are Syrian émigrés sympathetic to the Muslim Brotherhood, many of whom left Syria after the Ba'athist seizure of power in 1963. They organise charity, Arabic lessons and Quran study for immigrant families in Caracas and the oil towns.

They promote Islam as a complete way of life, social justice through religious charity and gradual moral reform rather than revolution. Hostile to the Ba'ath regime in Damascus and to communism, they look to the Gulf and Jordan for support. Their weight is small, but they shape the religious education of the younger generation.

13.name: Corporación Venezolana de Guayana
13.text:
The CVG, created in 1960 and headed by the engineer and general Rafael Alfonzo Ravard, is the state development agency building Ciudad Guayana, the Guri dam and the state steel and aluminium industry on the Orinoco. It is the showcase of Venezuelan planning.

Its technocrats believe the country should be run by engineers and planners rather than party bosses, using oil revenue to industrialise the interior. They prize efficiency, autonomy from Congress and foreign technical partnerships without political strings. Controlling vast budgets and enjoying the confidence of successive presidents, the CVG is a state within the state.

14.name: Opinión Nacional
14.text:
Opinión Nacional, founded in 1961 by Pedro Segnini La Cruz, is a small centre-right party that won a handful of seats in the 1968 elections. It stands outside the big party machines and offers itself as a voice for independents and the provincial middle class.

OPINA defends order, Catholic family values, moderate government and municipal autonomy, and criticises the patronage of both AD and COPEI. It favours neither superpower beyond Venezuela's traditional Western ties. Its leverage lies in its votes in a fragmented Congress, which make it a useful ally for a minority government.

15.name: Federación de Cámaras y Asociaciones de Comercio y Producción de Venezuela
15.native_full: Federación de Cámaras y Asociaciones de Comercio y Producción de Venezuela
15.text:
Fedecámaras, founded in 1944, is the peak federation of Venezuelan business, uniting the chambers of commerce, industry, agriculture and banking. Its members include the great Caracas family groups, importers and the industrialists who grew under protectionism.

It defends private enterprise, tariff protection for national industry and a cautious approach to oil policy, while opposing any extension of state ownership. Firmly pro-Western, it has the ear of every government, finances parties and newspapers, and can mobilise capital flight or investment strikes when it feels threatened.

16.name: Frente Nacional Democrático
16.text:
The FND was founded in 1964 around the writer and senator Arturo Uslar Pietri, who had run as an independent in 1963. After a strong start it declined and in 1968 joined the coalition behind Burelli Rivas, emerging much reduced.

It speaks for liberal professionals and businessmen: free enterprise, sound public finances, less patronage and 'sowing the oil', Uslar Pietri's call to invest petroleum wealth in productive industry rather than bureaucracy. Firmly pro-Western, it is a party of ideas rather than of masses, whose influence rests on Uslar Pietri's prestige and press columns.

17.name: Sociedad Venezolana de Ciencias Naturales
17.text:
The Venezuelan Society of Natural Sciences, founded in 1931, gathers naturalists, botanists and amateur explorers. Heirs of Henri Pittier, who inspired the country's first national park, its members have campaigned for the protection of the Ávila, the cloud forests and the Orinoco basin.

They call for new national parks, controls on deforestation and pollution from the oil industry, and scientific study of the Guayana region before dams and mines transform it. Non-partisan and small, they rely on scientific prestige, expeditions and newspaper columns to influence ministers and the public.

18.name: Movimiento Electoral del Pueblo
18.text:
The MEP was born in December 1967 when the educator Luis Beltrán Prieto Figueroa lost AD's presidential nomination and walked out with much of the party's left and labour wing. Prieto's 1968 candidacy split the AD vote and helped Caldera win; the MEP is now a significant force in Congress and the unions.

It advocates a socialist, non-aligned Venezuela: nationalisation of oil and iron, deeper agrarian reform, mass education and closer ties to Latin American and Third World movements. Its base is in teachers, trade unionists and AD dissidents, and its leverage lies in its union strength.

19.name: Movimiento de Izquierda Revolucionaria
19.text:
The MIR split from AD's youth wing in 1960 under Domingo Alberto Rangel, Simón Sáez Mérida and Américo Martín, and took up arms in the guerrilla war of the 1960s. Defeated in the field, it is now divided between those accepting Caldera's pacification and those still in the mountains.

Inspired by the Cuban revolution rather than by Moscow, it calls for a socialist revolution, expulsion of the oil companies and a break with the United States. Its strength lies in the universities and among radicalised young workers, but repression and internal splits have left it badly weakened.

20.name: Cruzada Cívica Nacionalista
20.text:
The Nationalist Civic Crusade is the movement of the deposed dictator Marcos Pérez Jiménez, living in exile in Madrid. In 1968 it stunned the establishment by taking the largest vote in Caracas and electing Pérez Jiménez senator, an election later annulled on technical grounds.

It appeals to nostalgia for the order, public works and full employment of the 1950s, blaming the party democracy for crime, corruption and guerrilla violence. Anti-communist and pro-Western, it draws on the urban poor and lower middle classes of Caracas, and its leverage lies in a protest vote both AD and COPEI fear.

21.name: Los de la Seguridad Nacional
21.english: The Men of the National Security
21.text:
The Men of the National Security are veterans of the Seguridad Nacional, the dreaded political police of the Pérez Jiménez dictatorship, dissolved in 1958. Its former chief Pedro Estrada lives in exile, while lesser agents have drifted into private security and the fringes of the right.

They despise parties and elections, want a hard nationalist state, a purged army and the extermination of the left. Discredited by torture and the prison camp of Guasina, they have no public following, but they keep contacts in the police and cultivate the hope of a strongman's return.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas Nacionales
22.text:
The National Armed Forces have stood behind the democratic order since 1958, after crushing both right-wing and leftist rebellions in the early 1960s and fighting the guerrillas for most of the decade. They are well paid, equipped from the United States and Europe, and trained in counterinsurgency.

The officer corps is professional and anti-communist, but it remembers a long tradition of military rule and watches the politicians with suspicion. Its leverage lies in its control of arms, the frontier with Colombia and Guyana, and its role as the final guarantor of the state should the parties fail.
22.wiki: National Bolivarian Armed Forces of Venezuela

23.name: Los Mantuanos
23.text:
The Mantuanos are the old creole families of Caracas, descendants of the colonial aristocracy whose ladies once wore the mantle to Mass. A few still guard Spanish titles, coats of arms and estates, and mingle with the large Spanish émigré community of the capital.

They cultivate Hispanidad, Catholic tradition and a nostalgic respect for the Spanish Crown, viewing the republic of parties and oil money as vulgar. They have no programme to restore a monarchy, but their social clubs, marriages and patronage still open doors in banking, the church and diplomacy.
